In addition, we will visualize linear transformations of the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$.
::: -->
:::

## Matrices as Functions

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

In $A{\bf x} = {\bf b},$ we can think of $A$ as a function that is "acting on" the vector $\bf x$ to create a new vector $\bf b$.

:::{.center-text}
<img src="images/linearity/2d-transform.jpeg" width=400 />

:::
This gives us a new way of thinking about solving $A \bf x = \bf b$: we are finding the vector(s) $\bf x$ that are transformed into $\bf b$ under the "action" of $A.$
:::

## Matrices as Functions

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
For example, consider $A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr}2&1&1\\3&1&-1\end{array}\right].$ Then $A \left[\begin{array}{r}1\\-4\\-3\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r}-5\\2\end{array}\right].$

In other words, if ${\bf x} = \left[\begin{array}{r}1\\-4\\-3\end{array}\right]$ and ${\bf b} = \left[\begin{array}{r}-5\\2\end{array}\right]$, then $A$ _**transforms**_ ${\bf x}$ into ${\bf b}$.


:::{.center-text}
<img src="images/linearity/3d-2d-transform.jpeg" width=800 />

:::
:::

## Matrices as Functions

:::{style="font-size: .7em;"}
$A$ took a vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and transformed it into a vector in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>
        How does this fact relate to the shape of \(A\)?
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```


:::{.notes}
$A$ is $2 \times 3$ -- that is, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}.$
:::

## Transformations

:::{style="font-size:.8em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p> <span class="label">Transformation</span>
        A <b>transformation</b> (or function/mapping) \(T\) from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is a rule that assigns to each vector \({\bf x}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) a vector \(T({\bf x})\) in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).<br>
        The set \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is called the <b>domain</b> of \(T\), and \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is called the <b>codomain</b> of \(T\).  
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```


__Notation__: $T: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ indicates $T$'s domain is $\mathbb{R}^n$ and the codomain is $\mathbb{R}^m.$

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>  <span class="label">Image</span>
         For \(\bf x\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n,\) the vector \(T({\bf x})\) is called the <b>image</b> of \(\bf x\) (under \(T\)). 
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

We sometimes write that $T$ maps ${\bf x}$ as ${\bf x} \mapsto T({\bf x})$.


```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>  <span class="label">Range</span>
         The set of all images \(T({\bf x})\) is called the <b>range</b> of \(T\).
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```
:::

## Linearity

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p> <span class="label">Linear transformation</span>
         A transformation \(T\) is <b>linear</b> if:
         <ol start="1">
<li>\(T({\bf u} + {\bf v}) = T({\bf u}) + T({\bf v}) \;\) for all \(\bf u, \bf v\) in the domain of \(T\);</li>
<li>\(T(c{\bf u}) = cT({\bf u}) \;\) for all scalars \(c\) and all \(\bf u\) in the domain of \(T\).</li>
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

Here, $T$ is a general function, not just matrix-vector multiplication.

This definition captures many transformations such as

$$
T(f) = \int_0^1 f(t) \,dt. 
$$

:::

## Linearity

:::{style="font-size:.8em"}
It is also possible to check if a transformation is linear using

$$
T(c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v}) = cT(\mathbf{u}) + dT(\mathbf{v}).
$$


If a transformation satisfies this equation for all $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ and $c, d,$ it must be a linear transformation.
<br><br>
Finally, it is important to note that if $T$ is a linear transformation, then

$$
T({\mathbf 0}) = T({\mathbf 0}) + T({\mathbf 0}), \quad \text{so} \quad T({\mathbf 0}) = {\mathbf 0}.
$$

:::

## Linearity

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Given a scalar $r$, define $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ by $T(\mathbf{x}) = r\mathbf{x}$. $T$ is called a __contraction__ when $0\leq r \leq 1$ and a __dilation__ when $r > 1$.

__Example__: Consider $r = 3$, and let us show that $T$ is a linear transformation.

Let $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ be in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $c, d$ be scalars.   Then

$$
\begin{align}
T(c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v}) &= 3(c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v}) \\
&= 3c\mathbf{u} + 3d\mathbf{v} \\
&= c(3\mathbf{u}) + d(3\mathbf{v}) \\
&= cT(\mathbf{u}) + dT(\mathbf{v})
\end{align}
$$

Thus, $T$ is a linear transformation because $T(c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v}) = cT(\mathbf{u}) + dT(\mathbf{v}).$
:::


## Linearity

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example__: Let $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ for some $\mathbf{b} \neq 0$. For example,  $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

<!-- When $T$ is applied, the entire 2-dimensional plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ is shifted one unit right and two units up. -->


This transformation is not linear. To see why, we can compare 

$$
\begin{align*}
&T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{b} \\
&T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v}) = (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b}) + (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + 2 \mathbf{b}.
\end{align*}
$$

Since $\mathbf{b} \neq 0$, those two expressions are not equal, so $T$ is _**not**_ a linear transformation.

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>
        Is the transformation \(T\left(\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_1 \end{bmatrix}\) linear?
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```


:::

## Matrix of a Linear Transformation{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 0.9em"}
Every linear transformation from vectors to vectors is a matrix multiplication.
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p> <span class="label">Theorem</span>
        Let \(T: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) be a linear transformation.   Then there is a unique matrix \(A\) such that:<br>
        &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;\(T({\bf x}) = A{\bf x} \;\;\; \mbox{for all}\; {\bf x} \in \mathbb{R}^n.\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

Let ${\bf e_j}$ denote the $j$th column of $I$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then ${\bf e_j}$ is a __standard basis vector__.

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
ax = dm.plotSetup(-3,3,-1,3,size=(4,4))
ax.plot([0],[1],'ro',markersize=8)
ax.arrow(0, 0, 1, 0, head_width=0.2, head_length=0.2, length_includes_head = True)
ax.arrow(0, 0, 0, 1, head_width=0.2, head_length=0.2, length_includes_head = True)
ax.text(0.25,1,'(0,1)',size=20)
ax.plot([1],[0],'ro',markersize=8)
ax.text(1.25,0.25,'(1,0)',size=20);
```

:::
:::

## Matrix of a Linear Transformation{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .9em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p> <span class="label">Standard matrix</span>
        The <b>standard matrix</b> of \(T\) is the \(m \times n\) matrix whose \(j\)th column is the vector \(T({\bf e_j})\). If we denote it by \(A\), then \(A = \left[T({\bf e_1}) \dots T({\bf e_n})\right].\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```


```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">

        a. Find the standard matrix representation \(A\) of \(T\).<br>
        b. Find a formula for \(T\left( \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}\right).\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```
